title: Least-Privilege Access for AI Agents in Accounting Software: Read, Write, Never Delete
summary: How to set AI agent permissions in accounting software: least-privilege tiers, no-delete defaults, segregation of duties and audit trails.
body_markdown:
**TL;DR:** An AI agent with write access to your accounting software should get the minimum access its tasks need: usually view, create and edit on specific record types, with no delete, no approval of its own work and no payment release. Run it under a dedicated service account, log every change, require a human to approve any change to its instructions in a separate system, and never bypass vendor-hosted or on-premise systems that block automated access.


The question finance teams ask most when an AI agent is proposed is not “is it accurate?” It is “how much can it do?” An agent that enters bills, codes bank transactions or creates estimates in QuickBooks Online, Xero or an ERP is, in the words directors often use, “as good as any staff member” once it has a login. That is exactly what makes them nervous. A staff member who deletes the wrong invoice makes one mistake. An agent with the same rights can make the same mistake two hundred times before lunch.


The answer is not to keep agents read-only forever, which removes most of their value. It is to scope their access deliberately. This guide sets out a practical permission model for finance teams granting AI agents write access to accounting systems: which tiers to allow, which to withhold, who approves what, and how to prove it to an auditor. For the wider governance picture, including risk committees and policy, see our[framework for AI governance in finance automation](https://peakflo.co/blog/ai-governance-finance-automation-compliance-frameworks) . This article stays focused on one question: what exactly the agent is allowed to touch.


## What Is Least-Privilege Access for AI Agents?


Least-privilege access for AI agents means giving an agent only the permissions required for its specific tasks, on the specific records it handles, for as long as it needs them. In accounting software, that typically means view, create and edit rights on a narrow set of transaction types, while deletion, approval, payment release and system configuration remain with named humans.


The principle is decades old. NIST defines[least privilege](https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/least_privilege) as a design principle in which each entity is granted the minimum system resources and authorisations needed to perform its function. What is new is the entity. An AI agent is neither a traditional integration, which does one fixed thing, nor a person, who exercises judgement within social and legal constraints. It reasons, chooses actions and calls tools, which is why the OWASP project lists[excessive agency](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm062025-excessive-agency/) as a top risk for LLM applications: too much functionality, too many permissions or too much autonomy.


For finance, the practical translation is simple. Decide the agent’s job first, then grant the narrowest access that lets it do that job, then add controls around the actions that remain risky.


## Why Is “As Good as Any Staff” the Wrong Mental Model?


Treating an AI agent like a staff member leads teams to give it a staff role, and staff roles are usually far broader than any single task requires. Agents act at machine speed and volume, do not get tired or suspicious, and follow instructions literally. Their access should be narrower than a person’s, not equal to it.


Three differences matter. First, **scale** : an agent processing a backlog of bank lines will repeat a flawed pattern across every line before anyone notices. Second, **instruction risk** : an agent’s behaviour can change when its prompt or rules change, or when a document it reads contains misleading content. Third, **attribution** : if the agent shares a login with the accounts executive, nobody can later tell who changed a figure.


A better model is a junior contractor on a tightly defined engagement. They may input and correct work in agreed areas. They cannot sign off their own work, delete records or move money. Everything they do is visible to their supervisor.


## What Permission Tiers Should Finance Teams Use?


Finance teams should think in six permission tiers: view, create, edit, delete, approve and pay. Most AI agents need only the first three, scoped to particular record types. Delete, approve and pay are high-consequence actions that should stay with humans by default and be granted to agents only for narrow, well-tested cases with compensating controls.


- **View** : read records, reports and attachments. Needed for almost every task, but still scope it; an agent creating estimates does not need payroll.
- **Create / input** : add new draft records such as bills, estimates, bank transaction matches or journal drafts.
- **Edit** : correct fields on records the agent or a person created, such as GL codes, tax codes, references and descriptions.
- **Delete / void / reverse** : remove or cancel posted records. High risk because it erases evidence and alters reported figures.
- **Approve** : move a record to approved or posted status. Must never apply to the agent’s own work.
- **Pay** : release payments or bank files. The highest-risk tier.


The matrix below shows how these tiers map to common agent tasks. Use it as a starting template and adjust per entity.


Agent task View Create Edit Delete Approve Pay


Create estimates from project data Yes Yes Yes (own drafts) No No No


Enter supplier bills from invoices Yes Yes Yes No No No


Code and match bank transactions Yes Yes Yes No No No


Suggest GL coding on non-PO invoices Yes No Yes (coding fields) No No No


Draft month-end accrual journals Yes Yes (draft) Yes (draft) No No No


Send payment reminders to customers Yes No Yes (notes, promise dates) No No No


Prepare payment batch Yes Yes (batch draft) Yes No No No


Manage users, chart of accounts, tax settings No No No No No No


Notice that the agent can prepare almost everything and finalise almost nothing. That is the point. Teams using[AI GL coding on non-PO invoices](https://peakflo.co/blog/ai-gl-coding-automation-non-po-invoices) see most of the time savings from the create and edit tiers alone.


## What Should the Default Permission Set Be?


The recommended default for an AI agent in accounting software is view plus create and edit on the transaction types it handles, with no delete, no approval and no payment release. This captures most of the productivity benefit, keeps every high-consequence action under human control, and gives you a clean baseline to widen from once the agent has a measured track record.


This matches what cautious finance leaders tend to ask for in their first conversation: the agent can view and input, it must not delete, and they want clarity on how much autonomy it has. Writing that down as a policy turns a vague worry into an enforceable control. A short policy statement might read:


```text
AGENT: bookkeeping-agent-01 (service account)
ALLOW: view, create, edit ON bills, estimates, bank_transactions, journal_drafts
DENY:  delete, void, reverse ON all records
DENY:  approve ON any record created or edited by this agent
DENY:  payment_release, user_admin, chart_of_accounts_edit, tax_settings_edit
ASK:   when confidence below threshold OR vendor not in master OR amount above limit
OWNER: Finance Manager (approves permission and instruction changes)
```


The “ask” line matters as much as the deny lines. A well-scoped agent should escalate uncertainty rather than guess, which is the core idea behind[human-in-the-loop AI for finance](https://peakflo.co/blog/human-in-the-loop-ai-finance-governance-framework) .


## Why Should Humans Own Deletions and Reversals?


Humans should own deletions and reversals because these actions destroy or alter evidence, change previously reported figures and can carry tax consequences. An agent that wrongly creates a record leaves a visible error that can be corrected. An agent that wrongly deletes one leaves a gap that may not be noticed until reconciliation or audit.


In practice, the agent can still help. It can identify a duplicate bill, explain why it thinks the bill is a duplicate, and place it in a “proposed for void” queue. A person reviews the evidence and performs the action. The agent saves the detective work; the human keeps the irreversible decision. The same logic applies to credit notes against posted invoices, reversing journals and unreconciling bank matches.


## How Does Segregation of Duties Apply to AI Agents?


Segregation of duties applies to AI agents by treating the agent as a distinct participant that cannot perform two conflicting steps in the same transaction. If the agent creates or edits a record, someone else approves it. If the agent prepares a payment batch, a different person releases it. The agent must never be able to approve its own work.


NIST describes[separation of duty](https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/separation_of_duty) as dividing critical functions among different parties so no single party can complete a sensitive process alone. Many teams forget that an agent with both create and approve rights collapses that separation even if no human is involved. Payments are the sharpest example: whichever platform handles[payment automation](https://peakflo.co/end-to-end-payment-automation) , the person releasing funds should not be the same identity that prepared the batch, and that identity should never be the agent.


There is a second, less obvious conflict: **the agent’s own instructions** . Many teams now use an automated reviewer, often an LLM-as-judge, to score agent output and suggest prompt improvements. That is useful. But if the same system can rewrite the agent’s instructions without human sign-off, the agent is effectively changing its own behaviour. Any change to prompts, rules or thresholds should be approved by a named human in a separate layer or system, with the previous version retained.


## Service Accounts or Shared Logins: Which Should an Agent Use?


An AI agent should always use a dedicated service account or a named API connection, never a shared staff login. A dedicated identity makes every action attributable to the agent, allows permissions narrower than any human role, and can be revoked instantly without locking out staff. Shared logins blur accountability and almost always over-grant access.


Accounting platforms differ in how fine-grained they are. Xero offers several[user roles and permissions](https://central.xero.com/s/article/User-roles-and-permissions-in-Xero) for people, and app connections use OAuth scopes. Intuit’s developer documentation on[QuickBooks Online OAuth scopes](https://developer.intuit.com/app/developer/qbo/docs/learn/scopes) shows that a single accounting scope can grant broad read and write access to accounting data. In other words, the ledger’s own controls may not express “create bills but never delete them”. That gap is usually closed in the automation layer between the agent and the ledger, which enforces the allowed actions before any API call is made. Ask any vendor exactly where that enforcement happens.


The comparison below shows why the access method matters as much as the permission level.


Access method Attribution Can be scoped narrower than a human role Revocation impact Recommended for agents


Shared staff login Actions look like a person’s No Locks out the staff member too No


Dedicated user seat for the agent Clear, per agent Only as narrow as the ledger’s roles Isolated to the agent Acceptable


OAuth app connection with scopes Clear, per app Partly, limited by scope design Isolated, instant Yes


OAuth connection plus action allow-list in the automation layer Clear, per action Yes, down to individual actions Isolated, instant Best practice


## What Should the Audit Trail Capture?


An AI agent audit trail should capture who acted (the agent’s identity), what changed (before and after values), when, which source data the agent relied on, why it chose that action, and who approved the result. Auditors should be able to reconstruct any figure the agent touched without interviewing anyone.


Minimum fields per action:


- Agent identity and version of its instructions at the time
- Timestamp and record identifier
- Before and after values for each field changed
- Source document or data reference
- Confidence score or short reasoning
- Approver identity and approval time, where applicable


Store this outside the agent’s own write scope so the agent cannot alter its log. This is consistent with the logging and access control expectations in[ISO/IEC 27001](https://www.iso.org/standard/27001) and the AICPA’s[SOC 2 trust services criteria](https://www.aicpa-cima.com/resources/landing/system-and-organization-controls-soc-suite-of-services) . Our guide to[data security in finance automation](https://peakflo.co/blog/data-security-finance-automation-vendor-invoice-protection) covers encryption and vendor assessment in more depth.


## What About Data the Agent Cannot Reach?


Some data sits in systems the agent should not access: vendor-hosted platforms whose provider does not permit third-party automation, or on-premise file servers that IT has not opened to outside services. Do not bypass these restrictions with borrowed credentials, screen scraping or unofficial connectors. Use approved exports, scheduled file drops or an agreed integration instead.


This comes up often in project-based businesses. For example, a professional services firm may hold project fees and durations in a vendor-hosted project platform and supporting files on an office NAS, while its ledger is in QuickBooks Online. The hosting vendor declines third-party AI access, and the IT provider says AI access is outside its scope. The tempting shortcut is to give the agent a staff login to the project platform. That breaches the vendor’s terms, creates an unmonitored access path and leaves no owner accountable.


The workable pattern is to let the agent work on cloud systems it is authorised to reach, and bridge the rest through controlled exports a person or scheduled job drops into an approved location. In Singapore, the PDPC’s[advisory guidelines on personal data in AI systems](https://www.pdpc.gov.sg/organisations/regulations-decisions/regulatory-guidance/advisory-guidelines-on-use-of-personal-data-in-ai-recommendation-and-decision-systems) and IMDA’s[Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI](https://www.imda.gov.sg/resources/press-releases-factsheets-and-speeches/press-releases/2026/new-model-ai-governance-framework-for-agentic-ai) both reinforce accountability for how data reaches AI systems.


## Which Risks Need Which Controls?


Each AI agent permission carries a specific risk, and each risk has a matching control. The table below pairs the most common failure modes with the control that contains them, so you can check whether your setup has a gap before the agent goes live.


Risk Example Primary control Detective control


Erroneous deletion Agent removes a “duplicate” that was valid No delete permission; void queue for humans Monthly deleted-record report


Self-approval Agent creates and approves a bill Approve denied on own records Approval-identity exception report


Unauthorised payment Agent releases a bank file No payment release; dual human approval Bank file audit log


Instruction drift Automated reviewer rewrites prompt Human approval in separate system Versioned prompt history


Over-broad access Agent uses staff login with admin rights Dedicated scoped service account Quarterly access review


Unapproved data access Agent scrapes a blocked vendor system Approved exports only Connection inventory review


Repeated pattern error Wrong GL code across hundreds of lines Confidence threshold and ask rule Sample review and judge scoring


Untraceable change Nobody knows who edited a figure Per-action audit log outside agent scope Audit trail completeness check

## Our Verdict: Let Agents Prepare, Let Humans Finalise


### Start with create and edit only if


- You are giving an agent write access for the first time
- Your auditors have not yet reviewed agent-based controls
- The agent handles high-volume, repeatable entries such as bills or bank lines
- You cannot yet measure the agent’s accuracy per task


### Consider widening access if


- The agent has several months of measured accuracy on a task
- Compensating controls such as dual approval and exception reports are in place
- The wider permission applies to low-value, easily reversible records


### Keep it manual if


- The action is deletion, payment release or user administration
- The data sits in a system whose owner has not approved automated access


**Our Recommendation:** Grant AI agents view, create and edit on the records their tasks require, deny delete, approve and pay by default, run them under dedicated service accounts with full logging, and require human approval in a separate system for any change to their instructions.


## Conclusion


AI agents earn their keep in accounting by doing the input work: entering bills, building estimates, coding bank lines and drafting journals. None of that requires the power to delete records, approve their own output or move money. Least privilege lets you capture the productivity while keeping every irreversible or high-consequence action with a person.


The model is straightforward. Define the agent’s tasks, map them to the minimum tier, run the agent under its own identity, separate preparation from approval, put instruction changes behind human sign-off, log everything and respect systems that are not open to automation. Done this way, the answer to “how much can the agent do?” is precise, documented and auditable.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### What does least privilege mean for an AI agent?


Least privilege means the AI agent receives only the minimum access needed to complete its assigned tasks, and nothing more. For an agent that enters bills or bank transactions, that usually means view, create and edit rights on specific record types, with no ability to delete records, approve its own work or release payments.


### Should an AI agent be allowed to delete records in accounting software?


In most finance teams, no. Deletion removes evidence and can break the audit trail, and reversals have tax and reporting consequences. The safer default is that the agent can flag a record for deletion or voiding, and a named human performs the deletion or reversal.


### What is the recommended default permission set for an AI bookkeeping agent?


A sensible default is view plus create and edit on the transaction types the agent handles, such as bills, estimates, bank transactions and journal drafts. Delete, approve, payment release, user management and chart-of-accounts changes stay with humans. Widen access only after the agent has a measured track record.


### Is an AI agent as risky as giving a staff member access?


It can be riskier if it is given a staff login, because it acts faster and at higher volume. It can be safer if it runs under a dedicated, scoped service account with every action logged, because its permissions are narrower than a typical staff role and its behaviour is fully reviewable.


### How does segregation of duties apply to AI agents?


The agent is treated as one participant in the process, so it cannot both perform and approve the same transaction. If the agent creates a bill, a human or a separate rule-based control approves it. If the agent prepares a payment batch, a different person releases it.


### Who should approve changes to an AI agent’s instructions?


A human owner should approve every change to the agent’s prompt, rules or instructions, in a separate layer or system from the one the agent runs in. This applies even when the change is suggested by an automated reviewer such as an LLM-as-judge, because instruction changes alter what the agent will do with its permissions.


### Should an AI agent use a shared login?


No. A shared login makes it impossible to tell whether a person or the agent made a change, and it usually carries far more access than the agent needs. Use a dedicated service account or API connection named for the agent, with its own scoped permissions and credentials that can be revoked independently.


### What should an AI agent audit trail record?


Each action should record the agent identity, timestamp, record affected, before and after values, the source document or data the agent relied on, its confidence or reasoning, and who approved the result. This lets auditors reconstruct why a figure changed without interviewing anyone.


### What if our data sits in a system that blocks AI agents?


Respect the block. If a hosting vendor or IT provider does not permit automated access, do not work around it with screen scraping or borrowed credentials. Use approved exports, scheduled file drops or an agreed integration, or keep that step manual until the system owner approves automated access.


### Do QuickBooks and Xero let you restrict what an AI agent can do?


Both offer user roles for people, and both use OAuth scopes for app connections, but API scopes are often broader than a finance team’s intended policy. For example, a single accounting scope can allow reading and writing many transaction types. Fine-grained limits such as no delete are usually enforced in the automation platform sitting between the agent and the ledger.


### Which standards cover access control for AI agents in finance?


Access control principles from ISO/IEC 27001 and the SOC 2 trust services criteria apply to AI agents in the same way they apply to human users and service accounts. In Singapore, PDPC guidance on personal data in AI systems and IMDA’s governance work on agentic AI are also relevant reference points.


### How often should AI agent permissions be reviewed?


Review them at least quarterly, alongside human user access reviews, and immediately whenever the agent is given a new task, connected to a new system or its instructions change materially. Remove any permission the agent has not used in the review period.
